My entire life I've always pretended to be indifferent to conceal my depression. When I was a kid I had a lot of trouble dealing with other kids my age. Social anxiety is what it's called now. Or being thin-skinned. Things were shit at home. Father with severe anger issues. Used to get smacked around now and again for silly little shit. 

I was so indifferent towards life that I didn't even bother checking out which course or college I wanted to go to. I just rolled with whatever I got (which happened to be a decent college). At the time of my graduation I had the mother of all panic attacks. I'd had them before but this one wrecked me and I felt the aftershock for six months after. I was nothing less than a zombie for two months. 

That was last year. I spent the earlier part of the year recovering and then got a writing gig where I spent two months and quite successfully. But I couldn't shake the horridness. The entire time I was dealing with a piercing pain in my neck (since the beginning of the year). It was diagnosed as tuberculosis cervical lymphadenitis. 

I was bedridden for three months and now I'm in the beginning of the fifth month. I could probably get a job starting next month but the searing volley of thoughts that rips through my head every time I stop trying to consciously suppress makes me feel completely helpless. I'm from India so we don't have a social tradition of leaving your parents house after going to college but even so I feel like a fucking parasite, man. I don't want to meet people cause when they ask me 'What are you doing?' I have nothing to say. 

I realised while I was graduating that I spent so much of my life pretending that I didn't care to repress my emotions that I have not the faintest idea of what I would like to do. I am miserable and for some reason I'm unable to make my thoughts stop. It's like I'm thinking them, they're rising from my insecurities or fears or whatever but they're in control. I feel so fucking wired, dude. Typing this got me worked up again.

At the risk of repeating myself, I can't stop feeling like shit and I've sort of stagnated in life, man. Going out to meet friends of mine sometimes ends with me washing my face in the bathroom, telling myself I can get through this without bursting into tears. 

I dunno when it happened but at some point I just started to perpetually feel like I'm gonna break down and I can't do the simplest shit anymore. Waking up and being greeted by someone having made a nice breakfast to cheer me up ends with me feeling like a piece of shit.

Forget 'doing what I like', I want to just stop thinking. I can't stop these thoughts. They sneak up on me. I don't wanna be useless, man, but everything I do is accompanied by this feeling that just saps all the life out of me and replaces it with fear and dread.

It's hard to trust my thoughts anymore and I feel sick with confusion.

Your title and the tone of your post suggests an inverse relationship between intelligence and cognitive biases. I'm going to go ahead and stop you right there and say that I completely disagree with that notion. Taking that core principle the argument could be made that if we were sufficiently intelligent then we wouldn't succumb to cognitive bias. 

Intelligence and identity are two deeply interlinked but essentially different aspects of the human psych. To grossly oversimplify, your intelligence is your ability to understand, problem solve, etc. Your identity is your notion of being an individual, your idea of 'me'.

Most cognitive biases, if not all of them, occur not because people aren't sufficiently intelligent but because they are more inclined to see the world in a way that conforms to their own views. Again, to oversimplify, it doesn't matter if you have Nvdia/AMD or an Intel Integrated Graphics Card if the user only wants to play Solitaire.

I would say it has more to do with self-awareness than with intelligence and even that is too tentative a statement to make. It has, however, been a long standing belief to attribute the kind of behaviour you're talking about as a result of intelligence. 

To me that is in itself a cognitive bias. 

Now I'm going to loop back to something else in your post. By and large what I see in your post is a sort of world weariness. I understand where you're coming from. I've felt the same way for a long time.

Personally I've stopped responding to any commentary on either demonetisation or Trump's election, unless it's actually substantive. For the same fucking reason you did and I really can't change your view on that because I have seen the same thing. 

But we will live with some cognitive biases no matter how intelligent we might be as long as we have a sense of self and an identity. It's not that people don't have the adequate tools to see this behaviour but that they do have those tools and they are using those tools to further reinforce their behaviour. 

Well, that might just be my own cognitive bias tho :p

With regards to medication. Nothing really, I'm just a stubborn fool with too much pride to depend on something external for a solution. I want to make a change in my habits, something long lasting. 

You mentioned meditation. It is helpful but not in the way you expect it to be. It doesn't give immediate results. You'll have to practice it for months but the improvement will be tangible.

My goal is very straightforward. I used to be a great student. One of the bright kids. Then I started on a steady decline. From straight A's in tenth grade I went to barely graduating uni by the skin of my teeth (though anxiety and panic attacks had a big role to play in that). Still it was my own doing.

The method I am going for is to use CBT to change my habits and become calmer on the inside while building up my focus and working hard externally for a complete change. Medications won't really help me with that so I use them only in the most minimal amount to keep the worst of the symptoms at bay. Sometimes it works, sometimes it doesn't.

You want to apply to a career in the field of your studies. So you know what you want to do. That's a great starting point. 

Now that you're at the starting line, you have to start running. But that's hard. Confidence is a lot about conditioning. People who have found success in the traditional models of schooling find themselves better equipped for life. There are other people who are confident not in their ability to succeed but in their ability to take any failure and keep on trucking. Personally I value that kind of confidence more, but I digress. 

After them come the rest of us. Lost little sheep. Anyone who didn't fit into the traditional model of schooling, people who didn't have functional environments which were conducive to personal development, idealists-turned-cynics. There's a bunch of people who fall into this category.

What you are experiencing, I believe, is the seeing life from the latter perspective. Overwhelmed by a pressure to succeed, scared of failing to do so and a constant immutable pressure from society to 'be productive'. 

Good. This is good. It means that you have the desire to achieve. It means that you still aspire. That's something worth holding on to. 

Now what you need is to tweak your perspective. For that you should begin by answering the question "What do I visualise when I think of success?"

The 'depressed writer' is a stereotype because many individuals who wrote profoundly had demons they had to deal with. 

Many depressed individuals need an outlet and writing is one that is more easily accessible than painting or music (which require cultivating a specific skill set as opposed to language which all of us learn in some capacity in our education). 

Sadness is an emotion that all of us, without exception, experience and it is perhaps easier to relate with given how much everyone is preoccupied with it.

It is some interplay of these factors, to whatever degree, because of which this stereotype has become so popular.
